'''''Ulmus pumila''''', the '''Siberian elm''', is a tree native to [[Asia]]. It is also known as the '''Asiatic elm''' and '''dwarf elm''', but sometimes mistakenly called the "Chinese" elm (''[[Ulmus parvifolia]]''). ''U. pumila'' has been widely cultivated throughout Asia, North America, Argentina, and southern Europe, becoming [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] in many places, notably across much of the United States.<ref>{{BONAP|ref|genus=Ulmus|species=pumila}}</ref><ref name=Hirsch,a>{{cite journal | last1 = Hirsch | first1 = H. | last2 = Brunet | first2 = J. | last3 = Zalapa | first3 = J. | last4 = Von Wehrden | first4 = H. | last5 = Hartmann | first5 = M. | last6 = Kleindienst | first6 = C. | last7 = Schlautman | first7 = B. | last8 = Kosman | first8 = E. | last9 = Wesche | first9 = K. | last10 = Renison | first10 = D. | last11 = Hensen | first11 = I. | year = 2017 | title = Intra- and interspecific hybridization in invasive Siberian elm | journal = Biol Invasions | volume = 19 | issue = 6| pages = 1889–1904 | doi=10.1007/s10530-017-1404-6| bibcode = 2017BiInv..19.1889H | hdl = 10019.1/122672 | s2cid = 42755808 | hdl-access = free }}</ref>

== Description ==

The Siberian elm is usually a small to medium-sized, often bushy, deciduous tree growing to {{Convert|25|m|abbr=on}} tall, the [[diameter at breast height]] to {{Convert|1|m|ftin|abbr=on}}. The bark is dark gray and irregularly longitudinally fissured. The [[branchlet]]s are yellowish gray, glabrous or pubescent, unwinged, and without a corky layer, with scattered lenticels. The winter buds are dark brown to red-brown, globose to ovoid. The [[petiole (botany)|petiole]] is {{Convert|4–10|mm|abbr=off|frac=4}} and pubescent; the leaf blade is [[leaf shape|elliptic-ovate to elliptic-lanceolate]], {{convert|2–8 × 1.2–3.5|cm|frac=8}},<ref> {{Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh |id=E00824809 }} Leaves specimen from Harbin, Manchuria (1953); [https://science.mnhn.fr/institution/mnhn/collection/p/item/p05539033?listIndex=145&listCount=547 Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris; herbarium specimen P06883116, labelled ''Ulmus'', Mongolia]</ref> the colour changing from dark green to yellow in autumn.<ref name="Fu">Fu, L., Xin, Y. & Whittemore, A. (2002). Ulmaceae, in Wu, Z. & Raven, P. (eds) ''Flora of China'', Vol. 5 (Ulmaceae through Basellaceae). Science Press, Beijing, and Missouri Botanical Garden Press, St. Louis, US. [http://flora.huh.harvard.edu/china/PDF/PDF05/Ulmus.pdf]</ref> The [[perfect flower|perfect]], [[apetalous]], [[wind-pollinated]] flowers bloom for one week in early spring, before the leaves emerge, in tight [[fascicle (botany)|fascicle]]s (bundles) on the last year's branchlets.<ref name="Flora of China">{{eFloras|2|200006332|Ulmus pumila|family=Ulmaceae|first1=Liguo|last1=Fu|first2=Yiqun|last2=Xin|first3=Alan|last3=Whittemore}}</ref><ref name="FNA">{{eFloras|1|200006332|Ulmus pumila |family=Ulmaceae |first=Susan L. |last=Sherman-Broyles}}</ref> Flowers emerging in early February are often damaged by frost (causing the species to be dropped from the Dutch elm breeding programme).<ref name=Went>Went, J. (1954). The Dutch Elm Disease – Summary of fifteen years' hybridization and selection work (1937–1952). ''European Journal of Plant Pathology''. 02(1954); 60(2): 109–1276.</ref> Each flower is about {{convert|3|mm|abbr=on|frac=64}} across and has a green [[calyx (botany)|calyx]] with four or five lobes, four to eight [[stamen]]s with brownish-red [[anther]]s,<ref name="illinois">{{Illinois Wildflowers |trees|plants|sb_elm|Siberian Elm (Ulmus pumila)|html=true|access-date=6 June 2023}}</ref> and a [[green]] [[pistil]] with a two-lobed [[style (botany)|style]].<ref name="FNA" /><ref>{{eFloras|1|134116|Ulmus |family=Ulmaceae |first=Susan L. |last=Sherman-Broyles}}</ref> Unlike most elms, the Siberian elm is able to [[self-pollinate]] successfully.<ref name=Townsend>{{cite journal|author=Townsend, A. M.|year=1975 |title=Crossability patterns and morphological variation among elm species and hybrids|journal=Silvae Genetica|volume=24|issue=1|pages=18–23|issn=0037-5349}}</ref>

The wind-dispersed [[Samara (fruit)|samarae]] are whitish tan, orbicular to rarely broadly obovate or elliptical, {{convert|1–2 × 1–1.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}}, and glabrous except for pubescence on the  stigmatic surface; the stalk is {{convert|1–2|mm|abbr=on|frac=128}}, and the [[perianth]] is persistent. The seed is at the centre of the samara or occasionally slightly toward the apex, but does not reach the apical notch. Flowering and fruiting occur from March to May. [[Ploidy]]: 2''n'' = 28.<ref name=Fu/> The tree also suckers readily from its roots.<ref name=Grbić>Grbić, M., Skočajić, D., Đukić, M., Đunisijević-Bojović, D., Marković, M. (2015). 'Mass clonal propagation of elm as a way for replacement of endangered autochthonous species'. p.62. ''Proceedings, International Conference Reforestation Challenges, 3–6 June 2015, Belgrade, Serbia.''</ref>

The tree is short-lived in temperate climates, rarely reaching more than 60 years of age, but in its native environment, may live between 100 and 150 years.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.northern.edu/natsource/TREESA1/Siberi1.htm |title=Untitled |access-date=2008-01-04 |archive-date=2007-11-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071113055509/http://www.northern.edu/natsource/TREESA1/Siberi1.htm }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.picsearch.com/imageDetail.cgi?id=icdtftmr0ZqPIpekvXObHiYqpqVcAOfXIT6vkvi-Mrg&width=1240&start=121&q=Ulmus|title=Pictures|access-date=2010-11-19|archive-date=2015-09-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924073121/http://www.picsearch.com/imageDetail.cgi?id=icdtftmr0ZqPIpekvXObHiYqpqVcAOfXIT6vkvi-Mrg&width=1240&start=121&q=Ulmus}}</ref> A giant specimen, {{Convert|45|km|abbr=on}} southeast of [[Khanbogt]] in the south [[Gobi]], with a girth of {{Convert|5.55|m|ftin|abbr=on}} in 2009, may exceed 250 years (based on average annual ring widths of other ''U. pumila'' in the area).{{citation needed|date=January 2017}}

== Taxonomy ==
The species was described by [[Peter Simon Pallas]] in the 18th century from specimens from [[Transbaikal]].

Two [[Variety (botany)|varieties]] were traditionally recognized: ''U. p. ''var.''  pumila'' and ''U. p.'' var. ''arborea'', but the latter is now treated as a cultivar, [[Ulmus pumila 'Pinnato-ramosa'|''U. pumila'' 'Pinnato-ramosa']].

== Distribution and habitat ==

The tree is native to [[Central Asia]], eastern [[Siberia]], the [[Russian Far East]], [[Mongolia]], [[Tibet]], northern [[China]], [[India]] (northern [[Kashmir]]), and [[Korea]].<ref name="Fu" /><ref name="Flora of China" /><ref>{{GRIN|id=40851|name=Ulmus pumila|access-date=8 September 2016}}</ref> It is the last tree species encountered in the semidesert regions of Central Asia.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Solla |first1=A. |last2=Martín |first2=J. A. |last3=Corral |first3=P. |last4=Gil |first4=L. |date=2005 |title=Seasonal changes in wood formation of ''Ulmus pumila'' and ''U. minor'' and its relation with Dutch elm disease |journal=New Phytologist |volume=166 |issue=3 |pages=1025–1034 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-8137.2005.01384.x |pmid=15869660|doi-access=free |bibcode=2005NewPh.166.1025S }}</ref>

=== Invasiveness and spontaneous hybridization ===
In North America, ''U. pumila'' has become an [[invasive species]] in much of the region from central Mexico<ref name="Todzia">{{cite journal |author1=Todzia, C. A. |author2=Panero, J. L. |name-list-style=amp |year=1998 |title=A new species of ''Ulmus'' (Ulmaceae) from southern Mexico and a synopsis of the species in Mexico |journal=Brittonia |volume=50 |issue=3 |pages=343–347 |doi=10.2307/2807778 |jstor=2807778 |bibcode=1998Britt..50..343T |s2cid=21320752}}</ref> northward across the eastern and central United States to [[Ontario]], Canada.<ref name="McIlvain">McIlvain, E. H. & Armstrong, C. G. (1965). Siberian Elm: A Tough New Invader of Grasslands. ''Weeds'', Vol. 13, No. 3 (July 1965), pp 278 – 279. [[Weed Science Society of America]] & [[Allen Press]].</ref> It also hybridizes in the wild with the native ''[[Ulmus rubra|U. rubra]]'' (slippery elm) in the central United States, prompting conservation concerns for the latter species.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=J. E. Zalapa |author2=J. Brunet |author3=R. P. Guries |date=June 28, 2008 |title=Isolation and characterization of microsatellite markers for red elm (''Ulmus rubra'' Muhl.) and cross-species amplification with Siberian elm (''Ulmus pumila'' L.) |journal=Mol Ecol Resour |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=109–12 |doi=10.1111/j.1471-8286.2007.01805.x |pmid=21585729 |bibcode=2008MolER...8..109Z |s2cid=7294817}}</ref><ref name="Elowsky">Elowsky, C. G., Jordon-Thaden, I. E., & Kaul, R. B. (2013). A morphological analysis of a hybrid swarm of native ''Ulmus rubra'' and introduced ''U. pumila'' (Ulmaceae) in southern Nebraska. ''Phytoneuron'' 2013-44: 1–23. {{ISSN|2153-733X}}.</ref> In South America, the tree has spread across much of the Argentine [[pampas]].<ref name="Villamil">Villamil, C. B., Zalba, S. M. ''Red de información sobre especies exóticas invasoras – I3N-Argentina'' Universidad Nacional del Sur Bahía Blanca, Argentina.</ref><ref name="Hirsch,c">Hiersch, H., Hensen, I., Zalapa, J. Guries, R. & Brunet, J. (2013). Is hybridization a necessary condition for the evolution of invasiveness in non-native Siberian elm? ''Abstracts. Third International Elm Conference 2013. The elm after 100 years of Dutch elm disease''. Florence, p45.</ref>

In Europe, it has spread widely in Spain, and hybridizes extensively there with the native [[field elm]] (''U. minor''),<ref>[http://www.cirrusimage.com/tree_hybrid_elm.htm ''U. carpinifolia''  × ''U. pumila'', Morton Arboretum, Illinois, cirrusimage.com]</ref> contributing to conservation concerns for the latter species.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cogolludo-Agustín |first1=Miguel ángel |last2=Agúndez |first2=Dolores |last3=Gil |first3=Luis |year=2000 |title=Identification of native and hybrid elms in Spain using isozyme gene markers |journal=Heredity |volume=85 |issue=2 |pages=157–166 |doi=10.1046/j.1365-2540.2000.00740.x |pmid=11012718 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2000Hered..85..157C }}</ref>  Research is ongoing into the extent of hybridisation with ''U. minor'' in Italy.<ref name="Brunet-et-al-2013">{{cite journal |last1=Brunet |first1=Johanne |last2=Zalapa |first2=Juan E. |last3=Pecori |first3=Francesco |last4=Santini |first4=Alberto |date=14 May 2013 |title=Hybridization and introgression between the exotic Siberian elm, ''Ulmus pumila'', and the native Field elm, ''U. minor'', in Italy |journal=Biol Invasions |volume=15 |issue=12 |pages=2717–2730 |doi=10.1007/s10530-013-0486-z |bibcode=2013BiInv..15.2717B |s2cid=14385250}}</ref> In the Netherlands, 1700 Siberian elms planted in error for field elm in 2016 in the Zalkerbos near [[Kampen, Overijssel]], were grubbed up because of invasiveness concerns and replaced in 2023 with native species.<ref>[https://kampenonline.nl/siberische-iep-verdwijnt-uiterlijk-maart-2023-uit-zalkerbos/ 'Siberian elm will disappear from Zalkerbos by March 2023 at the latest', kampenonline, 15 November 2022]</ref>

''U. pumila'' is often found in abundance along railroads and in abandoned lots and on [[disturbed ground]].  The gravel along railroad beds provides ideal conditions for its growth - well-drained, nutrient-poor soil, and high light conditions; these beds provide corridors that facilitate its spread.  It is found as high as 8000 feet in the Sandia Mountains in New Mexico and is invading coniferous forest there. New Mexico may be a center of genetic diversity in North America. Owing to its high sunlight requirements, it seldom invades mature forests, and is primarily a problem in cities and open areas,<ref name="National">National Audubon Society (2002). ''Field Guide to North American Trees'', Western Region, p. 419-420</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=''Ulmus pumila'' (PIER species info) |url=http://www.hear.org/pier/species/ulmus_pumila.htm |website=[[Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk]] project (PIER))}}</ref> as well as along transportation corridors.

The species is now listed in Japan as an alien species recognized as established in Japan or found in the Japanese wild.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Mito |first1=Toshikazu |last2=Uesugi |first2=Tetsuro |date=2004 |title=Invasive Alien Species in Japan: The Status Quo and the New Regulation for Prevention of their Adverse Effects |url=http://www.airies.or.jp/publication/ger/pdf/08-02-08.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120322025026/http://www.airies.or.jp/publication/ger/pdf/08-02-08.pdf |archive-date=2012-03-22 |access-date=2011-03-30 |website=Airies}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==

''U. pumila'' was introduced into Spain as an ornamental, probably during the reign of [[Philip II of Spain|Philip II]] (1556–98),<ref name="nature.com">{{cite journal|title=Identification of native and hybrid elms in Spain using isozyme gene markers|first1=Miguel Ángel|last1=Cogolludo-Agustín|first2=Dolores|last2=Agúndez|first3=Luis|last3=Gil|date=1 August 2000|journal=Heredity|volume=85|issue=2|pages=157–166|doi=10.1046/j.1365-2540.2000.00740.x|pmid=11012718|doi-access=free |bibcode=2000Hered..85..157C }}</ref> and from the 1930s into Italy.<ref name="Brunet-et-al-2013" /> In these countries, it has naturally hybridized with the field elm (''U. minor''). In Italy, it was widely used in viniculture, notably in the [[Po River]] Valley, to support the grape vines until the 1950s, when the demands of mechanization made it unsuitable.

Three specimens were supplied by the [[Späth nursery]] of Berlin to the [[Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh]] (RBGE) in 1902 as ''U. pumila'',<ref>{{Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh |id=E00824808 }} {{Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh |id=E00824813 }} ''U. pumila'' herbarium leaf-specimens, RBGE 1902: elmer.rbge.org</ref> in addition to specimens of the narrow-leaved ''U. pumila'' cultivar 'Pinnato-ramosa'.<ref name="Edinburgh">{{cite book |date=1902|title=Accessions book|publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh|pages=45, 47 |url=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Royal_Botanic_Garden_Edinburgh._(1902)._Accessions_book_pages_45,47.jpg}}</ref> One was planted in RBGE; the two not planted in the Garden may survive in Edinburgh, as it was the practice of the Garden to distribute trees about the city.<ref name="Edinburgh" /> [[Kew Gardens]] obtained specimens of ''U. pumila'' from the [[Arnold Arboretum]] in 1908 and, as ''U. pekinensis'', via the [[Veitch Nurseries]] in 1910 from [[William Purdom]] in northern China.<ref>Elwes and Henry (1913), p.1927</ref> A specimen obtained from Späth and planted in 1914 stood in the [[Ryston|Ryston Hall]] arboretum, [[Norfolk]],<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.rystonhall.co.uk/ |title=rystonhall.co.uk/ |access-date=2018-07-21 |archive-date=2019-01-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190126101143/http://www.rystonhall.co.uk/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> in the early 20th century.<ref name="Ryston">{{cite book| title=Ryston Hall Arboretum catalogue |date=c. 1920 |pages=13–14|url=https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ryston_Hall_Arboretum_Catalogue_c._1920_pages_13,14.jpg}}</ref> The tree was propagated and marketed by the Hillier & Sons nursery, [[Winchester, Hampshire]], from 1962 to 1977, during which time over 500 were sold.<ref name="Hillier,a">Hillier & Sons (1977). ''Catalogue of Trees & Shrubs''. Hillier, Ampfield, UK.</ref><ref name="Hillier,b">Hillier & Sons ''Sales inventory 1962 to 1977'' (unpublished).</ref> More recently, the popularity of ''U. pumila'' in the Great Britain has been almost exclusively as a [[bonsai]] subject, and mature trees are largely restricted to arboreta.{{citation needed|date=September 2016}} In the UK the [[Tree Register of the British Isles|TROBI]] Champions grow at [[Thorp Perrow Arboretum]], Yorkshire, {{convert|19|m|ftin|abbr=on}} × {{convert|70|cm|ftin|abbr=on}} in 2004, and at [[St Ann's Well Gardens, Hove]], Sussex {{convert|20|m|ftin|abbr=on}} × {{convert|60|cm|ftin|abbr=on}} in 2009.<ref name=Johnson>Johnson, O. (ed.). (2011). ''Champion Trees of Britain & Ireland''. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. {{ISBN|978-1-84246-452-6}}</ref>

''U. pumila'' is said to have been introduced to the US in 1905 by Prof. [[John George Jack]],<ref name="Leopold">{{cite journal|last=Leopold|first=D. J.|journal=Journal of Arboriculture|title=Chinese and Siberian elms|date=1980|volume=6|issue=7|pages=175–179|url=http://joa.isa-arbor.com/request.asp?JournalID=1&ArticleID=1664&Type=2|access-date=6 June 2023|via=Arboriculture & Urban Forestry Online}}</ref> and later by [[Frank Nicholas Meyer]], though 'Siberian elm' appears in some 19th-century US nursery catalogues.<ref>[https://archive.org/details/catalogueofornam1855hove/page/4 Hovey & Co., Boston, Mass., ''Catalogue of ornamental trees & shrubs, evergreens and climbing plants'', 1855, p.5]</ref> The tree was cultivated at the [[United States Department of Agriculture]] (USDA) Experimental Station at [[Mandan, North Dakota]], where it flourished.<ref name="Klingaman">Klingaman, G. (1999). Plant of the Week: Siberian Elm. ''Extension News'', University of Arkansas, Division of Agriculture.</ref> It was consequently selected by the USDA for planting in shelter belts across the prairies in the aftermath of the [[Dustbowl]] disasters, where its rapid growth and tolerance for drought and cold initially made it a great success. However, the species later proved susceptible to numerous maladies. Attempts to find a more suitable cultivar were initiated in 1997 by the Plant Materials Center of the [[USDA]], which established experimental plantations at [[Akron, Colorado]], and [[Sidney, Nebraska]]. The study, no. 201041K, was to conclude in 2020.{{citation needed|date=September 2016}} The US National Champion, measuring {{convert|33.5|m|ftin|abbr=on}} high in 2011, grows in [[Berrien County, Michigan]].<ref name=American>American Forests. (2012). The 2012 National Register of Big Trees.</ref><ref>[http://www.americanforests.org/our-programs/bigtree americanforests.org]</ref> Siberian elm was also introduced to Canada, among notable plantings being a 1 km avenue of some 130 ''U. pumila'' planted in the mid-20th century, spanning nine blocks of East 6th Avenue, Vancouver (2025).<ref>[https://placesthatmatter.ca/location/elms-of-east-6th/ 'The East 6th Avenue Elms'; placesthatmatter.ca]</ref>

The seeds lose their viability rapidly after maturity unless placed on suitable germination conditions or dried and placed at low temperatures.<ref name=Hirsch,b>Hirsch, H., Wypior, C., Wehrden, H., Wesche, K., Renison, D, and Hensen, I. (2012). Germination performance of native and non-native ''Ulmus pumila'' populations. ''Neobiota 15'', 53–68. 14 Dec. 2012.</ref> The species has a high sunlight requirement and is not shade-tolerant; with adequate light, it exhibits rapid growth.  The tree is also fairly intolerant of wet ground conditions, growing better on well-drained soils. While it is very resistant to drought and severe cold, and able to grow on poor soils, its short period of [[dormancy]], flowering early in spring followed by continuous growth until the first frosts of autumn,<ref name=Geng>{{cite book|author=Geng, M. A.|year=1989|title=A provenance test with elm (''Ulmus pumila'' L.) in China|publisher=Silvae Genetica|volume=32|pages=37–44}}</ref> renders it vulnerable to frost damage.

As an [[ornamental plant|ornamental]], ''U. pumila'' is a very poor tree, tending to be short-lived, with brittle wood and poor crown shape, but it has nevertheless enjoyed some popularity owing to its rapid growth and provision of shade. The Siberian elm has been described as "one of the world's worst...  ornamental trees that does not deserve to be planted anywhere".<ref name=Dirr>{{cite book|author=Dirr, M.|year=1975|title=Manual of Woody Landscape Plants|publisher=Stipes Publishing LLC.|place=[[Champaign, Illinois]]|isbn=0-87563-099-5}}</ref> Yet in the US during the 1950s, the tree was also widely promoted as a fast-growing hedging substitute for [[privet]], and as a consequence is now commonly found in nearly all states.<ref name="Klingaman" />

=== Cultivars ===
Valued for the high resistance of some clones to [[Dutch elm disease]], over a dozen selections have been made to produce hardy ornamental cultivars, although several may no longer be in cultivation:
{{#section:List of elm cultivars, hybrids and hybrid cultivars|Ulmus_pumila_cultivars}}

A variegated weeping elm, with cream, dark green, and light green variegation, is cultivated in China as ''Ulmus pumila'' 'Variegata'.<ref>[http://ppbc.iplant.cn/tu/14022232 Tree photo, ''Ulmus pumila'' 'Variegata', China; Plant Photo Bank of China, ppbc.iplant.cn]</ref><ref>[http://ppbc.iplant.cn/tu/15172072 Leaves photo 1, ''Ulmus pumila'' 'Variegata', China; Plant Photo Bank of China, ppbc.iplant.cn]</ref><ref>[http://ppbc.iplant.cn/tu/15172068 Leaves photo 2, ''Ulmus pumila'' 'Variegata', China; Plant Photo Bank of China, ppbc.iplant.cn]</ref><ref>[http://ppbc.iplant.cn/tu/15172483 Leaves photo 3, ''Ulmus pumila'' 'Variegata', China; Plant Photo Bank of China, ppbc.iplant.cn]</ref>

Some authorities consider the cultivar '[[Ulmus 'Berardii'|Berardii]]' a form of ''U. pumila''.<ref name="Green">{{cite journal |last=Green |first=Peter Shaw |author-link=Peter Shaw Green |date=1964 |title=Registration of cultivar names in ''Ulmus'' |url=https://archive.org/stream/arnoldiaarno_21#page/40/mode/2up/ |journal=Arnoldia |publisher=[[Arnold Arboretum]], [[Harvard University]] |volume=24 |pages=41–80 |access-date=16 February 2017 |number=6–8 |doi=10.5962/p.249479 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Krüssman1984">Krüssmann, Gerd, ''Manual of Cultivated Broad-Leaved Trees & Shrubs'' (1984 vol. 3)</ref> [[Ulmus × hollandica 'Nottingham'|Nottingham elm]], considered an ''[[Ulmus × hollandica]]'' by [[Richard Hook Richens|Richens]], was marketed from the 19th century as 'Siberian elm'.

=== Hybrid cultivars ===
* [[Ulmus 'Androssowii'|Androssowii]], [[Ulmus × arbuscula|''U.'' × ''arbuscula'']], [[Ulmus 'Fuente Umbria'|Fuente Umbria]], [[Ulmus 'Karagatch'|Karagatch]], [[Ulmus 'Toledo'|Toledo]]

The species has been widely hybridized in the United States and Italy to create robust trees of more native appearance with high levels of resistance to Dutch elm disease:
* [[Ulmus 'Arno'|Arno]], [[Ulmus 'Cathedral'|Cathedral]], [[Ulmus 'Coolshade'|Coolshade]], [[Ulmus 'Fiorente'|Fiorente]], [[Ulmus 'Homestead'|Homestead]], [[Ulmus 'Lincoln'|Lincoln]], [[Ulmus 'Morton Plainsman' Vanguard|Morton Plainsman = {{tdes|Vanguard|caps}}]], [[Ulmus 'Morton Stalwart' Commendation|Morton Stalwart = {{tdes|Commendation|caps}}]], [[Ulmus 'New Horizon'|New Horizon]], [[Ulmus 'Plinio'|Plinio]], [[Ulmus 'Rebona'|Rebona]], [[Ulmus 'Regal'|Regal]], [[Ulmus 'Recerta'|Recerta]], [[Ulmus 'Rosehill'|Rosehill]], [[Ulmus 'San Zanobi'|San Zanobi]], [[Ulmus 'Urban'|Urban]], [[Ulmus 'Willis'|Willis]], Dutch clone [[Ulmus × hollandica 'Vegeta'#Hybrid_cultivars|U.'260']] (not released to commerce).

Other hybrid cultivars involving crossings with ''U. pumila'':
* [[Ulmus 'Den Haag'|Den Haag]], [[Ulmus 'Sapporo Autumn Gold'|Sapporo Autumn Gold]]

== Uses ==
The unripe seeds have long been eaten by the peoples of [[Manchuria]], and during the [[Great Chinese Famine]], they also became one of the most important foodstuffs in the [[Harbin]] region. The leaves were also gathered, to the detriment of the trees, prompting a prohibition order by the authorities, which was largely ignored. The leaves eaten raw are not very palatable, but stewed and prepared with [[kaoliang]] or [[foxtail millet]] make a better-tasting and more filling meal.<ref name=Baranov>Baranov, A. L. (1962). On the economic use of wild plants in N. E. China. ''Quarterly Journal of the Taiwan Museum'', 15 (122), 1962, 107–115.</ref>

==In literature and travel writing==
[[File:Ulmus pumila 3.JPG|thumb|right|''U. pumila'' open woodland in the sandy steppe in Bayannuur sum, [[Bulgan Province]], Mongolia, 2008]]
The "dwarf-"<ref>Tolstoy, Leo, '' 'The Cossacks' and 'The Raid': a new translation by A.R. MacAndrew'' (New York, 1961)</ref> or "shrub-elms"<ref>Tolstoy, Leo, ''A Prisoner in the Caucasus and Other Stories'', trans. Angus Roxburgh (Moscow, 1983)</ref> of the [[North Caucasus]], along with other local flora, appear in the opening description of [[Leo Tolstoy|Tolstoy]]'s story [[The Raid (Tolstoy story)|"The Raid"]] (1853).

[[Nicholas Roerich]] describes a specimen discovered on his travels through Mongolia:<ref>de Roerich, G. (1931). ''Trails to Inmost Asia.'' Yale University Press</ref>
<blockquote>We are in the deserts of Mongolia. It was hot and dusty yesterday. From far away, thunder was approaching. Some of our friends became tired from climbing the stony holy hills of Shiret Obo. While already returning to the camp, we noticed in the distance a huge elm tree – ''karagatch'', - lonely, towering amidst the surrounding endless desert. The size of the tree, its somewhat familiar outlines attracted us into its shadow. Botanical considerations led us to believe that in the wide shade of the giant there might be some interesting herbs. Soon, all the co-workers gathered around the two mighty stems of the ''karagatch''. The deep, deep shadow of the tree covered about 50 feet across. The powerful tree-stems were covered with fantastic burr growths. In the rich foliage, birds were singing and the beautiful branches were stretched out in all directions, as if wishing to give shelter to all pilgrims.</blockquote>
